title: Treatment-related changes in disability, distress, and quality of life in cluster headache: the CHANGES Study (Cluster Headache Assessment of Noticeable Gains in Experienced Symptoms)
summary:
The disorder cluster headache
Cluster headache (CH) is a disorder which is characterized by recurring, unilateral headache attacks with a very high intensity of pain. The pain usually occurs in the eye socket area and is accompanied by vegetative symptoms such as watery eyes, a runny nose, or sweating on the face. A sense of inner restlessness and an urge to move are experienced alongside these symptoms. The attacks can last between 15 and 180 minutes and occur up to eight times a day. In addition to the pain, people with CH frequently experience distress due to the unpredictability of the attacks and sleep disturbance. This often results in anxiety, emotional stress, and a reduced quality of life. In many cases, people affected by cluster headaches also experience mental disorders, such as depression or anxiety disorder and are more likely to consume drugs such as cannabis and tobacco. The prevalence of this condition is between 0.1 and 0.2%, which means that one in every 500 to 1,000 people is affected.

Study situation
To date, most studies have assessed how treatment affects headache symptoms. Despite the severe psychological strain, little research has been conducted on how treatment affects general well-being and quality of life. There are three questionnaires that assess the burden of cluster headaches:
(i) the Cluster Headache Scales (CHS, Klan et al., 2020)
(ii) the Cluster Headache Quality of Life Scale (CH-QoL, Kuhn et al., 2024)
(iii) the Cluster Headache Impact Questionnaire (CHIQ; Kamm et al., 2022).
However, it has not yet been sufficiently clarified how well these questionnaires are suited to reliably measuring changes in disease-associated strain and disability. The CHANGES study therefore aims to assess how well the questionnaires can measure changes after routine treatment (in this case, at the Frankfurt Headache Center). To this end, patients will answer a battery of questionnaires at two measurement points: at the beginning of their treatment and 6 weeks later (so-called “pre-post design”). The survey will be conducted using the university-adapted version of the SoSci-Survey platform (survey duration 20-30 minutes each).

Aim
This research project aims to assess how strain, disability, and quality of life in cluster headache patients change as a result of routine outpatient treatment and how well the above-mentioned questionnaires can measure these changes. The CHANGES study is therefore intended to provide information on which instrument is suitable for reliably measuring treatment success.

interventions.name: Routine outpatient treatment at the Frankfurt Headache Center

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
• Confirmed diagnosis of episodic or chronic cluster headache according to ICHD-3 criteria of the International Headache Classification (IHS)
• The participant is starting a new medical treatment or changing an existing medical treatment (e.g., change in prophylactic medication)
• Informed consent has been obtained
Exclusion criteria:
• Lack of consent or lack of capacity to consent 
• Insufficient knowledge of German
